\chapter*{The Gurmukhi script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Gurmukhi script (reference)}
\markboth{Gurmukhi}{Gurmukhi}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — the lessons teach reading through real words. This page gathers the system and flags what is special about \textbf{Gurmukhi} and Punjabi.

\section*{How Gurmukhi works (the three facts)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \pa{ਕ} = ka, \pa{ਨ} = na, \pa{ਮ} = ma — written left to right under a connecting top line.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign changes it:} \pa{ਕਾ} kā · \pa{ਕਿ} ki · \pa{ਕੀ} kī · \pa{ਕੁ} ku · \pa{ਕੂ} kū · \pa{ਕੇ} ke · \pa{ਕੋ} ko. The signs themselves are \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} ā · \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} i · \textbf{\pa{ੀ}} ī · \textbf{\pa{ੁ}} u · \textbf{\pa{ੂ}} ū · \textbf{\pa{ੇ}} e · \textbf{\pa{ੋ}} o. A \emph{bindi} \pa{ਂ} or \emph{ṭippi} \pa{ੰ} nasalises the vowel.
  \item \textbf{Word-initial vowels ride a carrier.} Three bearer letters — \pa{ੳ} (u-series), \pa{ਅ} (a-series), \pa{ੲ} (i-series) — hold a vowel that starts a word: \pa{ਅ} + nothing = \emph{a}, \pa{ਆ} = \emph{ā}.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{What is special about Gurmukhi and Punjabi}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{The \emph{pair bindi} (a dot beneath)} marks Perso-Arabic sounds Punjabi borrowed: \pa{ਸ਼} \emph{sh}, \pa{ਖ਼} \emph{x/kh}, \pa{ਜ਼} \emph{z}, \pa{ਫ਼} \emph{f}, \pa{ਗ਼} \emph{ġ}. The script literally annotates its loanwords — a visible record of Punjab's two vocabularies.
  \item \textbf{Tone.} Punjabi is unusual among Indian languages in being \textbf{tonal} — the old voiced-aspirate letters (\pa{ਘ} \pa{ਝ} \pa{ਢ} \pa{ਧ} \pa{ਭ}) now trigger a low or high tone on the syllable rather than a breathy consonant. Picked up by ear; the lessons flag it only where it changes a word.
  \item \textbf{Two number/vocabulary streams.} Like Hindi and Urdu, Punjabi keeps parallel Sanskritic and Perso-Arabic words for many ideas (\emph{dhannavād} / \emph{shukrīā}).
\end{itemize}

\section*{Punjabi in the family}

Punjabi is \textbf{Indo-Aryan} (like Hindi, Marathi, Bengali — all descended from Sanskrit), spoken across Punjab in India and Pakistan. In India it is written in \textbf{Gurmukhi}, \textquotedblleft{}from the mouth of the Guru,\textquotedblright{} shaped by the second Sikh Guru, Angad, in the 16th century, to write the community's teachings; in Pakistan it is more often written in a Perso-Arabic script (\emph{Shahmukhi}) — a mirror of Punjabi's own twin inheritances. The lessons trace both the Sanskrit and the Persian threads.
